meta.provenance_note: Disease definitions, markers and high-risk indicators are taken verbatim from this workbook and are never paraphrased. The cohort rules that map laboratory patterns onto these rows are defined separately in config/cohorts/, each citing the clinical reference that establishes it, and each disease link quotes the Disease Master field that justifies it. Correctness is established by the technical validation suites in tools/validate.py: configuration integrity, evidence coverage, clinical test cases, consistency properties, end-to-end mapping reachability and parameter-count coverage. Output is disease-risk signalling, not diagnosis.

data_quality_notes.Observation: Related Profile mismatch not fixable by content alone
data_quality_notes.Detail: The stakeholder's starter list suggested Influenza, Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV), CMV Infection, Chikungunya, and Zika for the 'Viral Infections' profile. Checking the actual NG test list, 'Viral Infections' only contains Dengue NS1/IgM/IgG, Malaria (Vivax/Falciparum), Varicella Zoster IgG, and Typhoid antibody/Widal tests - none of the suggested viruses have a matching marker in this profile today.
data_quality_notes.Recommendation: Do not seed those 5 diseases under Viral Infections without matching lab tests. Only 'Varicella (Chickenpox)/Herpes Zoster' was added here since it has a direct marker (Varicella Zoster Ab IgG). If Influenza/EBV/CMV/Chikungunya/Zika testing is added to the NG catalog later, revisit this profile.

data_quality_notes.Observation: Viral Infections and Bacterial Infections profiles contain tests for diseases already mapped elsewhere
data_quality_notes.Detail: Dengue Fever, Malaria, and Typhoid Fever tests physically sit under 'Viral Infections' and 'Bacterial Infections', but those diseases are currently only tagged to 'Infectious Diseases' in the Related Profile(s) column of their existing rows.
data_quality_notes.Recommendation: Consider adding 'Viral Infections' and 'Bacterial Infections' as additional Related Profile(s) values on the existing Dengue Fever, Malaria, and Typhoid Fever rows (multi-profile tagging, same pattern already used elsewhere in this sheet) rather than creating duplicate disease rows.

data_quality_notes.Observation: Bacterial Infections profile only supports one confidently new disease
data_quality_notes.Detail: The stakeholder's starter list suggested Bacterial Pneumonia, Streptococcal Infection, and Bacterial Meningitis. The actual tests under 'Bacterial Infections' are Typhidot/Widal (Typhoid), H. pylori antigen/antibody tests, Urea Breath Test, and a generic Gram Stain - none specific to pneumonia, strep, or meningitis.
data_quality_notes.Recommendation: Only 'Peptic Ulcer Disease/Gastritis (H. pylori-associated)' was added as a new row, cross-linked to the existing H. pylori Infection entry. Pneumonia/Strep/Meningitis were not added since there is no supporting marker in this profile; a Gram Stain alone is too non-specific to anchor a confident disease-level entry.

diseases.name: Allergic Asthma

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe acute attack
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe acute attack

marker_tokens: Specific IgE panel for inhalant allergens

fields.Definition: A form of asthma triggered by allergen exposure, causing airway inflammation and narrowing.
fields.Common Symptoms: Wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, coughing (especially at night or with exertion)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE panel for inhalant allergens; Total IgE
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction, correlated with allergen sensitization testing
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated specific IgE to common triggers with recurrent wheeze/breathlessness
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe acute attack
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, manageable with trigger avoidance and inhaled therapy; can be well controlled long-term
fields.Possible Complications: Severe asthma exacerbation, airway remodeling with poorly controlled long-term disease
fields.External Risk Factors: Allergen exposure (dust mite, pollen, mold, pet dander), air pollution, smoking
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of asthma or other atopic conditions
fields.Other Important Factors: Often begins in childhood; frequently coexists with allergic rhinitis and eczema
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Non-allergic asthma, COPD, vocal cord dysfunction
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Allergen avoidance, controller medication adherence, avoiding smoking/secondhand smoke
fields.Recommended Next Step: Pulmonologist/allergist consult; emergency care for severe attacks
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE panel for common inhalant allergens
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical exam correlated with allergen sensitization testing
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated specific IgE to inhalant allergens with matching eye symptoms
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – manage symptoms

fields.External Risk Factors: Pollen, dust, pet dander exposure
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of allergic conditions
fields.Other Important Factors: Frequently coexists with allergic rhinitis
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Infectious conjunctivitis, dry eye syndrome
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Allergen avoidance, avoiding eye rubbing
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist/ophthalmologist consult if persistent

diseases.name: Allergic Rhinitis

urgency.raw: Routine – manage symptoms

marker_tokens: Specific IgE panel for common inhalant allergens (pollen

fields.Definition: An allergic inflammation of the nasal passages triggered by airborne allergens such as pollen, dust mites, or pet dander.
fields.Common Symptoms: Sneezing, runny/blocked nose, itchy eyes/nose, watery eyes, postnasal drip
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE panel for common inhalant allergens (pollen, dust mite, pet dander)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Skin prick testing or specific IgE blood testing correlated with symptom history
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated specific IgE to common inhalant allergens with matching symptom pattern
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – manage symptoms
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic but well controlled with allergen avoidance and medication; may improve or persist over years
fields.Possible Complications: Sinusitis, disrupted sleep, worsened asthma control
fields.External Risk Factors: Exposure to pollen, dust mites, mold, pet dander; air pollution
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of allergic conditions (atopy) — asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis
fields.Other Important Factors: Often begins in childhood/adolescence; frequently coexists with asthma and eczema
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis, common cold, sinusitis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Allergen avoidance/environmental control (dust mite covers, air filtration)
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist consult for persistent or severe symptoms; consider immunotherapy
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

diseases.name: Anaphylaxis

urgency.raw: Emergency

marker_tokens: specific IgE testing after recovery to identify the trigger

fields.Definition: A rapid-onset, severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction affecting multiple body systems at once.
fields.Common Symptoms: Sudden hives, swelling of face/throat, difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, dizziness, loss of consciousness
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Serum tryptase (if drawn during/shortly after the event); specific IgE testing after recovery to identify the trigger
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical diagnosis based on rapid multi-system symptom onset after allergen exposure
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Any history of a rapid multi-system reaction following exposure to a known/suspected allergen
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Excellent with prompt treatment (epinephrine); risk of recurrence with re-exposure to trigger
fields.Possible Complications: Airway obstruction, cardiovascular collapse, death if untreated
fields.External Risk Factors: Exposure to known trigger (food, insect sting, medication, latex)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of severe allergic reactions
fields.Other Important Factors: Can occur at any age; history of asthma increases severity risk
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Vasovagal syncope, panic attack, other causes of acute breathlessness
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Strict avoidance of known trigger; carry emergency epinephrine auto-injector
fields.Recommended Next Step: Immediate emergency care (epinephrine); allergist follow-up for trigger identification
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

diseases.name: Atopic Dermatitis/Eczema

urgency.raw: Routine – manage symptoms

marker_tokens: specific IgE panel if trigger allergen suspected

fields.Definition: A chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition associated with an overactive immune/allergic response and skin barrier dysfunction.
fields.Common Symptoms: Itchy, dry, inflamed skin; red patches typically in skin folds (elbows, knees); worsens with scratching
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Total IgE; specific IgE panel if trigger allergen suspected
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical diagnosis based on appearance and history; IgE testing supportive, not required
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated total/specific IgE with characteristic chronic itchy rash pattern
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – manage symptoms
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic with flares and remissions; many children improve with age, some carry it into adulthood
fields.Possible Complications: Skin infection (from scratching), sleep disruption, progression of the 'atopic march' to asthma/allergic rhinitis
fields.External Risk Factors: Dry climate, harsh soaps/detergents, stress, certain fabrics
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Strong family history of atopy (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis); filaggrin gene mutations
fields.Other Important Factors: Most commonly begins in infancy/early childhood
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Contact dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal skin infection
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Regular moisturizing (skin barrier support), avoiding known irritants/triggers
fields.Recommended Next Step: Dermatologist/allergist consult for persistent or severe cases
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

fields.Definition: Recurring hives (itchy raised welts) lasting more than six weeks, often without an identifiable single trigger.
fields.Common Symptoms: Itchy raised welts that come and go, sometimes with swelling (angioedema)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Total IgE; specific IgE panel if a trigger is suspected; thyroid antibodies (autoimmune association)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical diagnosis based on duration/pattern; investigation for underlying autoimmune or physical trigger if persistent
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Recurrent hives beyond 6 weeks without a clear external trigger
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – manage symptoms; urgent if angioedema affects airway
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Often self-limiting over months to years, but can persist; generally manageable with antihistamine therapy
fields.Possible Complications: Angioedema (airway swelling, rare but serious), significant quality-of-life impact
fields.External Risk Factors: Stress, heat/cold exposure, certain medications (NSAIDs)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Association with autoimmune thyroid disease in some patients
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women; can be linked to underlying autoimmune conditions
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Acute urticaria, mastocytosis, vasculitis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Identify and avoid specific triggers where found; manage underlying autoimmune conditions
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist/dermatologist consult for persistent cases

urgency.base: Routine to urgent depending on reaction severity
urgency.raw: Routine to urgent depending on reaction severity

fields.Definition: An immune-mediated adverse reaction to a specific medication, distinct from a typical side effect.
fields.Common Symptoms: Skin rash/hives, itching, swelling, fever; severe reactions can include anaphylaxis or organ involvement
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE testing where available (limited for many drugs); tryptase if reaction was severe
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical history correlation; specialist-supervised skin testing or graded drug challenge for select drugs
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Clear temporal relationship between drug exposure and reaction onset
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine to urgent depending on reaction severity
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Generally good with avoidance of the culprit drug; cross-reactivity with related drugs possible
fields.Possible Complications: Anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (rare, severe)
fields.External Risk Factors: Exposure to the specific medication or drug class
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Certain HLA gene variants increase risk for specific drug reactions
fields.Other Important Factors: Common culprits include antibiotics (especially penicillins) and NSAIDs
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Non-allergic drug side effect, viral exanthem
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Document and avoid the confirmed allergen drug and related drug class; medical alert bracelet for severe reactions
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist consult for reaction workup and safe-drug alternatives

fields.Definition: An immune reaction to a specific food protein, ranging from mild skin symptoms to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
fields.Common Symptoms: Hives, swelling (lips/face/throat), vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing; severe cases progress to anaphylaxis
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE panel for common food allergens (peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg, shellfish, wheat)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Specific IgE/skin prick testing correlated with reaction history; oral food challenge in specialist setting for confirmation
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated specific IgE to a food allergen with a clear history of reaction on exposure
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if anaphylaxis occurs
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Some childhood food allergies (milk, egg) are often outgrown; others (peanut, shellfish) tend to persist lifelong
fields.Possible Complications: Anaphylaxis, nutritional deficiency from avoidance diets
fields.External Risk Factors: Early/late food introduction patterns in infancy (evolving evidence), cross-contamination exposure
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of food allergy or other atopic conditions
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in children; some allergies persist into adulthood
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Food intolerance (non-immune, e.g., lactose intolerance), oral allergy syndrome
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoidance of confirmed trigger food; carry emergency epinephrine if history of severe reaction
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist consult; emergency action plan if severe reaction history

urgency.raw: Routine for local reactions; emergency if systemic/anaphylactic

fields.Definition: An allergic reaction to insect venom (bee, wasp, hornet), ranging from local swelling to systemic anaphylaxis.
fields.Common Symptoms: Large local swelling at sting site, or systemic hives/breathing difficulty/dizziness in severe reactions
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Specific IgE to relevant insect venom
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Specific IgE or venom skin testing correlated with reaction history
fields.High-Risk Indicators: History of a systemic reaction to a sting, or elevated venom-specific IgE
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine for local reactions; emergency if systemic/anaphylactic
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Good with avoidance and, for at-risk individuals, venom immunotherapy which is highly effective
fields.Possible Complications: Anaphylaxis on repeat sting
fields.External Risk Factors: Outdoor activity in areas with stinging insects
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not strongly hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Risk of a severe reaction increases after a prior systemic reaction
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Local infection/cellulitis at sting site
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoidance of nests/hives, carry emergency epinephrine if prior systemic reaction
fields.Recommended Next Step: Allergist consult; consider venom immunotherapy after a systemic reaction

urgency.raw: Routine to monitor; urgent during acute hemolytic episode

fields.Definition: An inherited enzyme deficiency that makes red blood cells vulnerable to breakdown (hemolysis) under oxidative stress, such as certain foods, infections, or drugs.
fields.Common Symptoms: Usually asymptomatic until triggered; then jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, pallor after a trigger exposure
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Quantitative G6PD enzyme assay (best done when not in an acute hemolytic episode)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low quantitative G6PD enzyme level
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine to monitor; urgent during acute hemolytic episode
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Generally good with trigger avoidance; acute episodes are self-limited if trigger removed
fields.Possible Complications: Acute hemolytic anemia, neonatal jaundice/kernicterus in newborns
fields.External Risk Factors: Fava beans, certain antimalarials/antibiotics/sulfa drugs, infections
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: X-linked inheritance; much more common and severe in males; family history relevant
fields.Other Important Factors: Higher prevalence in African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and South/Southeast Asian populations
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other hemolytic anemias, autoimmune hemolysis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoidance of known trigger foods/drugs once diagnosed
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hematologist consult if recurrent episodes
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

urgency.raw: Routine – treat and monitor

fields.Definition: The most common form of anemia, caused by insufficient iron to produce adequate hemoglobin.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath, dizziness, brittle nails, pica (craving non-food items)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Iron, TIBC, UIBC, Ferritin, Transferrin Saturation
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Low ferritin with low serum iron and high TIBC; CBC showing microcytic hypochromic anemia
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low Ferritin with Low Iron and elevated TIBC/UIBC
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – treat and monitor
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Fully correctable with iron repletion once cause is identified and addressed
fields.Possible Complications: Severe fatigue, heart strain if prolonged and severe, developmental delay in children
fields.External Risk Factors: Poor dietary iron intake, chronic blood loss (GI bleeding, heavy menstruation), vegetarian diet without supplementation
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare hereditary iron metabolism disorders
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and young children
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia trait
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Iron-rich diet, screening in pregnancy and high-risk groups
fields.Recommended Next Step: Identify and treat underlying cause of blood loss if present
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

fields.Definition: An inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells become rigid, sickle-shaped, and prone to blocking blood flow.
fields.Common Symptoms: Episodic severe pain (crises), fatigue, jaundice, swelling in hands/feet, frequent infections
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Sickle Cell Solubility Test, Hemoglobin Electrophoresis
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Hemoglobin electrophoresis showing HbS pattern
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Positive sickling test confirmed on electrophoresis
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management; urgent during a pain crisis
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic lifelong condition; management has greatly improved life expectancy

fields.Definition: A state of higher-than-normal blood glucose that has not yet reached the threshold for diabetes, signaling elevated future risk.
fields.Common Symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7-6.4%
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Fasting glucose in impaired range, especially combined with obesity or family history
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – lifestyle intervention
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reversible with lifestyle change; roughly a third progress to type 2 diabetes without intervention
fields.Possible Complications: Progression to type 2 diabetes, early vascular changes
fields.External Risk Factors: Sedentary lifestyle, high-calorie diet, obesity
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of diabetes
fields.Other Important Factors: Age 45+, history of gestational diabetes, PCOS
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Diabetes Mellitus, normal glucose variation
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Structured weight loss and exercise program (most effective intervention); dietary carbohydrate moderation

fields.Definition: A serious, acute complication of diabetes where a severe insulin shortage causes the body to break down fat for fuel, producing dangerous ketone acid buildup.
fields.Common Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath, confusion, extreme thirst
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Blood Sugar (Random), Ketone (urine), pH, Electrolytes (Sodium, Potassium)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Blood glucose >250 mg/dL with ketonemia/ketonuria and metabolic acidosis (blood gas)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: High glucose with positive urine ketones and low blood pH
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Life-threatening if untreated; full recovery expected with prompt hospital treatment
fields.Possible Complications: Cerebral edema (esp. in children), severe electrolyte imbalance, shock
fields.External Risk Factors: Missed insulin doses, infection, undiagnosed diabetes, acute illness
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Underlying Type 1 diabetes genetic risk
fields.Other Important Factors: Most common in Type 1 diabetes but can occur in Type 2 under stress/illness
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, alcoholic ketoacidosis, sepsis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Consistent insulin adherence, sick-day glucose/ketone monitoring
fields.Recommended Next Step: Immediate emergency care

fields.Definition: A condition where one or more parathyroid glands produce excess parathyroid hormone, raising blood calcium and affecting bone density.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often asymptomatic, detected via routine calcium testing; when symptomatic — fatigue, bone pain, kidney stones, constipation, mood changes ('stones, bones, groans, and moans')
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Elevated calcium with elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone (PTH) level
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated calcium with elevated PTH, especially with low phosphorus
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – manage; urgent if severe hypercalcemia
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Generally excellent with surgical removal of the overactive gland (primary form); good long-term outlook with monitoring for mild cases
fields.Possible Complications: Osteoporosis, kidney stones, kidney impairment, cardiovascular effects of chronic hypercalcemia
fields.External Risk Factors: Not strongly linked to external factors; low vitamin D can contribute to secondary hyperparathyroidism
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare hereditary endocrine tumor syndromes (MEN1, MEN2A)
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women, particularly postmenopausal
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, vitamin D toxicity, secondary hyperparathyroidism from kidney disease
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate vitamin D status to avoid secondary hyperparathyroidism
fields.Recommended Next Step: Endocrinologist consult; consider parathyroid imaging and surgical evaluation

fields.Definition: An acute, self-limiting viral liver infection typically spread through contaminated food or water.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine, low-grade fever

fields.External Risk Factors: Contaminated food/water, poor sanitation, travel to endemic areas
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: More common where sanitation is poor; vaccine-preventable
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Hepatitis B/C/E, drug-induced liver injury
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Hepatitis A vaccination, safe food/water practices, hand hygiene

fields.Other Important Factors: Vaccine-preventable; chronic risk highest when infection occurs in infancy/early childhood
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Hepatitis A/C/D, autoimmune hepatitis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Hepatitis B vaccination, safe sex practices, screening blood products

fields.Definition: The absence of menstrual periods for three or more months in someone who previously had regular cycles (secondary amenorrhea), or absence by age 15 (primary amenorrhea) — this entry covers the general presentation before a specific cause is identified.
fields.Common Symptoms: Absence of expected menstrual periods; may accompany symptoms of the underlying cause (weight change, hair growth, headaches, galactorrhea)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: LH, FSH, Prolactin, TSH, Testosterone (initial hormonal workup panel)

fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – identify underlying cause
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Depends entirely on the underlying cause once identified (see PCOS, Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, menopause)
fields.Possible Complications: Infertility, bone density loss if prolonged low-estrogen state, complications of the underlying cause
fields.External Risk Factors: Significant weight change, excessive exercise, high stress
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Depends on underlying cause
fields.Other Important Factors: This is a presenting sign rather than a single disease — always investigate for the specific cause
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Pregnancy, PCOS, Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, premature ovarian insufficiency, menopause
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Depends on underlying cause
fields.Recommended Next Step: Gynecologist/endocrinologist consult for stepwise hormonal workup

fields.Definition: Absence of menstrual periods caused by disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, typically due to excessive exercise, low body weight, or significant stress.

fields.Other Important Factors: Common in competitive athletes and those with disordered eating patterns
fields.Differential Diagnoses: PCOS, pregnancy, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, premature ovarian insufficiency
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate nutrition and energy balance relative to exercise level

fields.Definition: A condition of excess prolactin hormone, which can disrupt menstrual cycles, fertility, and cause milk production unrelated to breastfeeding.

fields.Differential Diagnoses: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, medication effect, pituitary tumor

fields.Definition: The natural transition marking the end of a woman's reproductive years, driven by declining ovarian hormone production.
fields.Common Symptoms: Irregular periods, hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, vaginal dryness, sleep disturbance
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Elevated FSH with low estradiol in the context of menstrual pattern change and age (clinical diagnosis primarily)

fields.Differential Diagnoses: Thyroid dysfunction, pregnancy, other causes of irregular periods
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Not preventable (natural process); bone/cardiovascular health monitoring recommended around this transition

fields.Definition: A common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age, causing irregular periods, excess androgen levels, and often polycystic ovaries.
fields.Common Symptoms: Irregular/absent periods, excess facial/body hair, acne, weight gain, difficulty conceiving

fields.External Risk Factors: Obesity worsens symptoms and insulin resistance
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of PCOS or type 2 diabetes
fields.Other Important Factors: Very common — affects a substantial proportion of women of reproductive age
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Weight management to reduce symptom severity and metabolic risk

fields.Definition: The onset of puberty at an abnormally early age (typically before 8 in girls, 9 in boys), driven by premature hormonal activation.
fields.Common Symptoms: Early breast development/menstruation (girls), early testicular/genital growth (boys), rapid height growth, early pubic/underarm hair

fields.External Risk Factors: Obesity is associated with earlier puberty onset
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of early puberty; certain genetic conditions
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in girls; can be idiopathic or due to an underlying central nervous system cause
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Normal early but physiologic puberty, adrenal or gonadal tumor (peripheral precocious puberty)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No proven primary prevention

fields.Related Markers/Tests: Sputum/urine analysis where relevant, inflammatory markers
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Sputum AFB smear/culture, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, or chest imaging with clinical correlation
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Persistent cough with weight loss and positive sputum test
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management; urgent if disseminated/severe
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Curable with full-course multi-drug therapy; poor prognosis if treatment incomplete or drug-resistant
fields.Possible Complications: Lung damage, disseminated (miliary) TB, drug-resistant TB, extrapulmonary TB (including renal TB)
fields.External Risk Factors: Crowded living conditions, malnutrition, close contact with active TB case
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No strong direct hereditary link; immune-related genetic susceptibility factors exist
fields.Other Important Factors: Higher risk with HIV co-infection, diabetes, immunosuppression
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Pneumonia, lung cancer, other chronic lung conditions
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: BCG vaccination (in endemic regions), early case detection and treatment, contact tracing

fields.Definition: A bacterial infection anywhere in the urinary system, most commonly the bladder, but can ascend to the kidneys.
fields.Common Symptoms: Painful/burning urination, urinary frequency/urgency, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, lower abdominal pain; fever and flank pain if kidney involvement

fields.Definition: A life-threatening condition where the body's response to an infection injures its own tissues and organs, potentially leading to organ failure.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fever or low body temperature, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, confusion, low blood pressure, extreme illness
fields.Related Markers/Tests: CBC (WBC), CRP/inflammatory markers if available, blood culture
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Blood culture identifying the causative organism, combined with clinical organ dysfunction criteria (e.g., SOFA score)

fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Serious — mortality risk rises sharply with delayed treatment; good outcomes with early recognition and treatment
fields.Possible Complications: Septic shock, multi-organ failure, death
fields.External Risk Factors: Any untreated or undertreated infection, especially in immunocompromised or elderly patients
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not directly hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Higher risk in very young, elderly, immunocompromised, or chronically ill patients
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Severe allergic reaction, other causes of shock
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Prompt treatment of infections, especially in high-risk individuals

fields.Definition: A progressive, long-term loss of kidney function over months to years, often silent until advanced.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often asymptomatic early; later fatigue, swelling (legs/ankles), decreased urine output, itching, nausea
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Serum Creatinine, Blood Urea, Glomerular Filtration Rate, Albuminuria

fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; urgent if rapidly declining
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Progressive; can lead to dialysis/transplant if unmanaged, but progression can be slowed significantly with treatment
fields.Possible Complications: End-stage renal disease, cardiovascular disease, anemia, bone disease, and — commonly — secondary hyperlipidemia/dyslipidemia driven by the kidney dysfunction itself (a downstream consequence rather than a separate diagnosis)
fields.External Risk Factors: Uncontrolled diabetes/hypertension, NSAID overuse, dehydration
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of kidney disease, polycystic kidney disease
fields.Other Important Factors: Risk increases with age, diabetes, and hypertension as compounding factors
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Acute kidney injury, nephrotic syndrome
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Blood pressure and blood sugar control, avoiding nephrotoxic drugs, hydration

fields.Definition: A form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the buildup of uric acid crystals in joints, most classically the big toe.

fields.Definition: A specific pattern of abnormal blood lipids — high triglycerides, low HDL, and small dense LDL particles — that strongly raises cardiovascular risk, commonly seen with insulin resistance.

fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Lipid panel showing the characteristic high triglyceride/low HDL/small dense LDL pattern

fields.External Risk Factors: Sedentary lifestyle, high-carbohydrate/high-sugar diet, obesity, alcohol excess

fields.Other Important Factors: Frequently coexists with Metabolic Syndrome, Diabetes, and PCOS
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Familial hypercholesterolemia (a distinct primary lipid disorder)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Diet low in refined carbohydrates, regular exercise, weight management

fields.Synonyms / AKA: CAD, Coronary heart disease, Ischemic heart disease
fields.Definition: A condition where the coronary arteries supplying the heart become narrowed or blocked, usually by plaque buildup, restricting blood flow to the heart muscle.
fields.Common Symptoms: Chest pain/pressure (angina), shortness of breath, fatigue with exertion, pain radiating to arm/jaw
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, Triglycerides, Troponin, Homocysteine, APO A, APO B
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: ECG, stress testing, coronary angiography/CT coronary angiogram
fields.High-Risk Indicators: High LDL + Low HDL + High Triglycerides together (Critically High per risk summary); High Troponin (acute); High Homocysteine; High APO B / Low APO A ratio
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency if acute chest pain/suspected heart attack; otherwise needs monitoring
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Progressive if risk factors unmanaged; modifiable with lifestyle change, medication, and procedures when needed
fields.Possible Complications: Heart attack (myocardial infarction), heart failure, arrhythmia, sudden cardiac death
fields.External Risk Factors: Smoking, high saturated fat diet, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, high alcohol intake
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of early heart disease/stroke
fields.Other Important Factors: Age, gender (post-menopausal risk change), existing diabetes/hypertension as compounding factors
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Musculoskeletal chest pain, GERD, anxiety, pulmonary causes
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Smoking cessation, heart-healthy diet, regular exercise, blood pressure/lipid/glucose control
fields.Recommended Next Step: Immediate care for acute chest pain; cardiologist consult for risk management

fields.Related Markers/Tests: Fasting Glucose, Triglycerides, HDL, Blood Pressure, Waist circumference (if tracked)

fields.Definition: A mosquito-borne parasitic infection (Plasmodium species) causing cyclical fever and, in severe forms, life-threatening organ complications.
fields.Common Symptoms: Cyclical high fever with chills/rigors, headache, sweating, fatigue, nausea; in severe cases confusion, jaundice, breathing difficulty
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Malaria antigen test (rapid diagnostic test), peripheral blood smear
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) identifying the parasite, or positive rapid antigen test
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Positive blood smear/antigen test, especially with high parasite density or signs of severe disease
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe malaria (organ involvement)
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Excellent with prompt appropriate antimalarial treatment; severe malaria can be fatal if delayed

fields.External Risk Factors: Mosquito exposure in endemic areas, travel to endemic regions without prophylaxis

fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Mosquito nets, repellents, antimalarial prophylaxis for travel to endemic areas, vector control

fields.Definition: Inflammation of the pancreas, which can be acute (sudden, often resolving) or chronic (progressive, permanent damage).
fields.Common Symptoms: Severe upper abdominal pain (often radiating to back), nausea, vomiting, fever (acute); weight loss and fatty stools (chronic)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Elevated amylase/lipase with characteristic abdominal pain; CT/MRI for confirmation and complication assessment
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Amylase markedly elevated with severe abdominal pain
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency if acute and severe
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Acute cases often resolve fully with supportive care; chronic pancreatitis causes progressive, often irreversible damage
fields.Possible Complications: Pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, diabetes (from chronic damage), malnutrition
fields.External Risk Factors: Heavy alcohol use, gallstones, high triglycerides, certain medications
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Hereditary pancreatitis (rare, PRSS1 gene mutation)
fields.Other Important Factors: Gallstones and alcohol account for most cases
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Peptic ulcer disease, cholecystitis, bowel obstruction
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Limit alcohol intake, manage gallstones and triglycerides
fields.Recommended Next Step: Immediate care if severe acute pain; gastroenterologist consult for chronic disease

fields.External Risk Factors: Unprotected sex, multiple partners
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not hereditary; congenital transmission possible from untreated mother to fetus
fields.Other Important Factors: Screening especially important in pregnancy and high-risk populations

fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Safe sex practices, partner screening/treatment, prenatal screening

fields.Synonyms / AKA: Human Immunodeficiency Virus infection, AIDS (late stage)
fields.Definition: A viral infection that progressively attacks the immune system (specifically CD4 cells), potentially advancing to AIDS if untreated.
fields.Common Symptoms: Acute: flu-like illness. Chronic: often asymptomatic for years. Late-stage (AIDS): recurrent infections, significant weight loss

fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, manageable condition with near-normal life expectancy on modern antiretroviral therapy; untreated, progresses to AIDS
fields.Possible Complications: Opportunistic infections, AIDS-defining illnesses, certain cancers
fields.External Risk Factors: Unprotected sex, needle sharing, mother-to-child transmission, unscreened blood products
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Early diagnosis and treatment initiation greatly improves outcomes
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other causes of immunosuppression, acute viral illness
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Condom use, PrEP for high-risk individuals, needle safety, screening blood products

fields.Definition: Inadequate levels of folate, a B vitamin essential for cell division and DNA synthesis, particularly important in pregnancy.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, pale skin, glossitis, irritability, poor growth (in children)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Low serum/red cell folate level
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low folate with macrocytic anemia on CBC
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – treat and monitor
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Readily reversible with supplementation
fields.Possible Complications: Megaloblastic anemia; neural tube defects if deficient during early pregnancy
fields.External Risk Factors: Poor diet, alcohol use, malabsorption disorders (celiac disease)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: MTHFR gene variants can affect folate metabolism
fields.Other Important Factors: Critical in women of childbearing age/pregnancy for fetal neural tube development
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Vitamin B12 deficiency (similar presentation)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Folate-rich diet; folic acid supplementation pre-conception and in early pregnancy
fields.Recommended Next Step: Folic acid supplementation per clinician guidance

fields.Definition: Inadequate levels of vitamin B12, essential for red blood cell formation and neurological function.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, pale skin, tingling/numbness in hands and feet, memory issues, glossitis, mood changes
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Low serum B12; methylmalonic acid/homocysteine (if available) for borderline cases
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Vitamin B12 level in the deficient range with macrocytic anemia on CBC
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – treat and monitor
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reversible with supplementation if caught before permanent nerve damage occurs
fields.Possible Complications: Peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (if prolonged/severe), megaloblastic anemia
fields.External Risk Factors: Vegan/vegetarian diet without supplementation, alcohol use
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Pernicious anemia (autoimmune) has familial autoimmune association
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in elderly, strict vegetarians/vegans, and after gastric/bowel surgery
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Folate deficiency, pernicious anemia, hypothyroidism
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate dietary B12 or supplementation, especially for plant-based diets
fields.Recommended Next Step: B12 supplementation; investigate for pernicious anemia if unexplained

fields.Definition: Inadequate levels of vitamin D, a hormone-like vitamin essential for calcium absorption and bone health.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, bone pain, muscle weakness, mood changes; often asymptomatic
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below reference range
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Vitamin D level in the deficient range, especially with elevated PTH or low calcium
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine – treat and monitor
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Easily correctable with supplementation and sun exposure
fields.Possible Complications: Osteomalacia/rickets, osteoporosis, increased fracture risk
fields.External Risk Factors: Limited sun exposure, dark skin, poor diet, obesity, malabsorption

fields.Other Important Factors: More common in elderly, indoor-dwelling individuals, and those in northern latitudes
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Osteoporosis, hypoparathyroidism
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate sun exposure, dietary/supplemental vitamin D, fortified foods
fields.Recommended Next Step: Vitamin D supplementation per clinician guidance

fields.Common Symptoms: Numbness/tingling, vision problems, muscle weakness, balance issues, fatigue, cognitive changes
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: MRI brain/spine with contrast showing demyelinating lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands

fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; urgent neurology referral on new focal deficits
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, relapsing-remitting in most cases; progressive in a subset
fields.Possible Complications: Progressive disability, vision loss, mobility loss if poorly controlled
fields.External Risk Factors: None well established; possible link to low Vitamin D, smoking, prior EBV infection
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of MS or other autoimmune disease
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women; onset typically 20-40 years
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, other autoimmune encephalitides, vitamin B12 deficiency
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No proven prevention; smoking cessation and Vitamin D sufficiency are commonly advised

fields.Common Symptoms: Drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty swallowing/chewing, muscle weakness worsening with activity
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Repetitive nerve stimulation test, single-fiber EMG, correlated with AChR antibody positivity
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Positive AChR antibody with fatigable muscle weakness
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if respiratory/swallowing muscles involved (myasthenic crisis)
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, manageable with treatment; can fluctuate
fields.Possible Complications: Myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure if untreated
fields.External Risk Factors: None well established
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of autoimmune disease
fields.Other Important Factors: Can coexist with thymoma; more common in women under 40 and men over 60
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, thyroid eye disease, botulism
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No specific prevention; treatment adherence and infection avoidance to prevent crisis
fields.Recommended Next Step: Neurologist referral; emergency care if breathing/swallowing affected

fields.Definition: A rare autoimmune disorder where the immune system attacks peripheral nerves, often following an infection, causing rapidly progressive weakness.
fields.Common Symptoms: Ascending weakness/numbness starting in the legs, difficulty walking, in severe cases breathing difficulty
fields.Related Markers/Tests: CSF Proteins (albuminocytologic dissociation), Anti-ganglioside antibodies where available
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Nerve conduction studies showing demyelination; CSF analysis
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated CSF protein with normal cell count following recent infection, with progressive weakness
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency - can progress to respiratory failure within days
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Acute onset, usually monophasic; most recover over weeks to months
fields.Possible Complications: Respiratory failure, prolonged weakness, autonomic instability
fields.External Risk Factors: Often preceded by infection (e.g., Campylobacter, viral illness)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No strong genetic pattern
fields.Other Important Factors: Requires hospitalization for monitoring in early phase
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Transverse myelitis, myasthenia gravis, acute spinal cord compression
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No established prevention; prompt treatment of triggering infections
fields.Recommended Next Step: Emergency neurology/hospital admission

fields.Definition: Neurological dysfunction caused by antibodies that cross-react with brain tissue, sometimes triggered by an underlying tumor.
fields.Common Symptoms: Confusion, seizures, memory problems, abnormal movements, personality changes
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1), Anti-Ri (ANNA-2), Amphiphysin Antibody, CASPR2, AMPA receptor antibodies
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: MRI brain, CSF analysis, antibody panel, and screening for an underlying malignancy
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Positive paraneoplastic antibody panel (Hu/Ri/Amphiphysin/CASPR2/AMPA) with matching neuro-psychiatric symptoms
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs urgent workup; emergency if seizures or rapidly progressive confusion
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Variable; depends on underlying cause and how quickly treated
fields.Possible Complications: Permanent cognitive/neurological deficit if underlying tumor and antibody process not addressed
fields.External Risk Factors: None well established
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: None well established
fields.Other Important Factors: Often signals an occult malignancy requiring cancer screening
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Viral encephalitis, primary psychiatric illness, metabolic encephalopathy
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No established prevention; early detection of underlying malignancy is protective

fields.Definition: A neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
fields.Common Symptoms: Seizures (convulsive or non-convulsive), loss of awareness, unusual sensations preceding a seizure (aura)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Carbamazepine (Tegretol) level for those on treatment
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: EEG showing epileptiform activity; MRI brain to rule out structural cause
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Recurrent unprovoked seizures confirmed on EEG; drug levels used for monitoring, not diagnosis
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if seizure lasts over 5 minutes (status epilepticus) or new-onset seizure
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Often chronic; many achieve good control with medication
fields.Possible Complications: Injury during seizures, status epilepticus, medication side effects
fields.External Risk Factors: Head injury, stroke, brain infection as underlying causes in some cases
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of epilepsy in a subset of cases
fields.Other Important Factors: Medication adherence critical; certain triggers (sleep deprivation, alcohol) can provoke seizures
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Syncope, psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, hypoglycemia
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Medication adherence, trigger avoidance, safety precautions
fields.Recommended Next Step: Neurologist referral for EEG/MRI and medication management

fields.Definition: Damage to peripheral nerves causing weakness, numbness, and pain, most often in the hands and feet.
fields.Common Symptoms: Numbness, tingling, burning pain, weakness, often starting in the feet
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Nerve conduction studies/EMG
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low B12 or poorly controlled diabetes together with sensory symptoms in a stocking-glove pattern
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine to needs monitoring depending on severity/cause
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Often chronic; progression depends on underlying cause being controlled
fields.Possible Complications: Foot ulcers, falls, chronic pain if underlying cause unmanaged
fields.External Risk Factors: Alcohol use, toxin exposure
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare hereditary neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth) in a subset
fields.Other Important Factors: Very commonly caused by diabetes or B12 deficiency - treat underlying cause first
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, hereditary neuropathy
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Glycemic control, B12 repletion, alcohol moderation

fields.Possible Complications: Chronic daily headache, medication-overuse headache
fields.External Risk Factors: Stress, poor sleep, certain foods/alcohol, hormonal changes
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Strong family history pattern
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women; can worsen or improve with hormonal changes/pregnancy
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Tension headache, cluster headache, secondary headache from structural cause
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Trigger avoidance, sleep hygiene, stress management

fields.Common Symptoms: Abdominal pain, constipation, fatigue, irritability, in children: developmental delay/learning difficulty
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Confirmed elevated blood lead level on repeat testing with exposure history
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated blood Lead level, especially in children or occupationally exposed adults
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if very high levels with encephalopathy
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reversible if exposure source removed early; can cause permanent effects if prolonged/high exposure
fields.Possible Complications: Cognitive impairment (especially in children), anemia, kidney damage
fields.External Risk Factors: Occupational exposure (batteries, paint, smelting), old paint/pipes, contaminated water
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component
fields.Other Important Factors: Children more vulnerable to neurodevelopmental effects than adults
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Iron deficiency anemia (can coexist), other heavy metal toxicity
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Identify and remove exposure source; occupational safety measures

fields.External Risk Factors: High mercury fish consumption, occupational exposure, dental/industrial exposure
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component
fields.Other Important Factors: Pregnant women and children more vulnerable to neurodevelopmental effects
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other heavy metal toxicity, primary neurological disease
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Limit high-mercury fish intake, occupational safety measures

fields.Differential Diagnoses: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (non-bacterial), BPH, STDs
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Safe sexual practices, prompt treatment of UTIs

fields.Definition: Inflammation of the epididymis (and sometimes the testicle), usually caused by bacterial infection, including sexually transmitted organisms.
fields.Common Symptoms: Testicular/scrotal pain and swelling, fever, painful urination
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Positive culture identifying causative organism with antibiotic sensitivity; STD screening in sexually active men
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Positive bacterial growth on semen/urine culture with matching clinical presentation
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly for severe swelling/pain to rule out testicular torsion

fields.Possible Complications: Abscess, infertility if recurrent/untreated, chronic pain
fields.External Risk Factors: Unprotected intercourse (especially with chlamydia/gonorrhea), recent UTI or catheterization
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component
fields.Other Important Factors: Testicular torsion must be urgently excluded as it is a surgical emergency
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Testicular torsion, testicular tumor, mumps orchitis
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Safe sexual practices, prompt STD treatment

fields.Definition: Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox on primary infection and, upon reactivation later in life, shingles.
fields.Common Symptoms: Chickenpox: itchy vesicular rash, fever. Shingles: painful vesicular rash in a band-like pattern
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Clinical diagnosis in most cases; IgG confirms past exposure/immunity rather than acute infection (IgM/PCR needed for acute diagnosis, not currently in this panel)

fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine for chickenpox in healthy individuals; needs monitoring/seek care promptly for shingles or if immunocompromised
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chickenpox usually self-limited in children; shingles can cause prolonged nerve pain (post-herpetic neuralgia)
fields.Possible Complications: Bacterial skin superinfection, post-herpetic neuralgia, rare complications in immunocompromised/pregnant patients
fields.External Risk Factors: Immunosuppression increases shingles risk and severity
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component
fields.Other Important Factors: Vaccine-preventable; more severe in adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other vesicular rashes (HSV, hand-foot-mouth disease)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Varicella vaccination; zoster vaccination in older adults
fields.Recommended Next Step: Dermatology/infectious disease referral if severe or immunocompromised

fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other causes of chronic liver disease, other movement disorders
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No established prevention; early diagnosis and treatment prevent progression

fields.Common Symptoms: Poor wound healing, hair loss, diarrhea, reduced taste/smell, skin rash
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Serum zinc level (preferred over urine for diagnosis) correlated with clinical signs
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low zinc level with matching clinical signs, especially in malabsorption or poor dietary intake

fields.Possible Complications: Impaired immunity, delayed wound healing if prolonged
fields.External Risk Factors: Poor diet, malabsorption, high alcohol intake, chronic diarrhea
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare inherited zinc malabsorption disorders (acrodermatitis enteropathica) in infants

fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component

fields.Definition: Impaired blood clotting due to reduced production of clotting factors by a diseased liver.
fields.Common Symptoms: Easy bruising, bleeding gums, prolonged bleeding from cuts, in severe liver disease: GI bleeding
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Prolonged PT/INR in the setting of confirmed liver disease, not correcting with vitamin K alone
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Prolonged PT/INR with abnormal LFTs (low albumin, elevated bilirubin/transaminases)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly with active bleeding or acute liver failure
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reflects severity of underlying liver disease; can improve if liver disease is treated/reversible

fields.External Risk Factors: Alcohol use, viral hepatitis, other chronic liver disease causes
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component (unless underlying liver disease is hereditary)
fields.Other Important Factors: PT/INR is also used as a marker of liver synthetic function severity (e.g., in cirrhosis scoring)
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant use, other clotting factor deficiencies

fields.Definition: Routine monitoring of blood clotting time in patients on warfarin or similar anticoagulants to ensure the dose keeps them in a safe therapeutic range.
fields.Common Symptoms: Usually asymptomatic; bruising/bleeding if over-anticoagulated, clotting events if under-anticoagulated
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: INR compared against the patient's target therapeutic range for their indication
fields.High-Risk Indicators: INR outside the prescribed therapeutic range (too high = bleeding risk, too low = clotting risk)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if INR very high with bleeding, or very low with clotting symptoms
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Ongoing monitoring need for as long as anticoagulation continues
fields.Possible Complications: Bleeding (over-anticoagulation) or clot/stroke (under-anticoagulation)
fields.External Risk Factors: Diet (vitamin K intake), alcohol, interacting medications
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Genetic variants (e.g., CYP2C9, VKORC1) can affect warfarin sensitivity
fields.Other Important Factors: Requires regular follow-up testing; not a standalone diagnosis
fields.Differential Diagnoses: N/A - this is a monitoring context, not a differential diagnosis situation
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Consistent diet, medication reconciliation, regular INR checks
fields.Recommended Next Step: Managing physician/anticoagulation clinic follow-up

fields.Definition: A serious condition where widespread clotting activation consumes clotting factors and platelets, causing both clotting and bleeding throughout the body.
fields.Common Symptoms: Bleeding from multiple sites, bruising, confusion, organ dysfunction symptoms depending on cause
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Prolonged PT and PTT with low platelets and low fibrinogen in the correct clinical context (sepsis, trauma, malignancy)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Prolonged PT/PTT with thrombocytopenia and elevated D-dimer in a critically ill patient
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Emergency - life-threatening condition
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Acute and life-threatening; prognosis depends on treating the underlying trigger
fields.Possible Complications: Multi-organ failure, severe bleeding, death if untreated
fields.External Risk Factors: Underlying sepsis, trauma, malignancy, or obstetric complications trigger DIC - not a primary risk factor condition
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: No significant genetic component
fields.Other Important Factors: Almost always occurs as a complication of another severe acute illness
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Liver failure coagulopathy, primary massive hemorrhage, thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No independent prevention - managing the triggering illness is key
fields.Recommended Next Step: Emergency/ICU admission

diseases.name: Rh Incompatibility/Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn

urgency.escalation: emergency-level neonatal care if severe hemolysis at birth
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring throughout pregnancy; emergency-level neonatal care if severe hemolysis at birth

fields.Disease/Medical Condition: Rh Incompatibility/Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn
fields.Definition: A condition where an Rh-negative mother develops antibodies against an Rh-positive fetus's blood, which can cause the baby's red blood cells to be destroyed in a subsequent pregnancy.
fields.Common Symptoms: In the newborn: jaundice, anemia, in severe cases hydrops fetalis; the mother is typically asymptomatic
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Blood Group, Rh Factor, Rh Factor Quantitative
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Maternal antibody screen (indirect Coombs test), fetal/newborn direct Coombs test
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus, especially with a positive antibody screen in a prior or current pregnancy
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring throughout pregnancy; emergency-level neonatal care if severe hemolysis at birth
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Preventable with anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM); can be serious if unmanaged in an already-sensitized pregnancy
fields.Possible Complications: Severe newborn anemia, jaundice/kernicterus, hydrops fetalis
fields.External Risk Factors: Not applicable in the traditional lifestyle sense - obstetric risk factor is prior sensitizing pregnancy/procedure
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Blood type is inherited; risk is specific to Rh-negative mother with Rh-positive father/fetus
fields.Other Important Factors: Routine pregnancy blood typing and anti-D prophylaxis timing are critical
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other causes of neonatal jaundice/anemia (e.g., G6PD deficiency, ABO incompatibility)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis during pregnancy per protocol
fields.Recommended Next Step: Obstetrician/maternal-fetal medicine referral
fields.Source / Reference: Not yet sourced - AI-drafted from general clinical knowledge; pending citation during clinical review.

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly/emergency if very high BP with symptoms (hypertensive emergency)
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly/emergency if very high BP with symptoms (hypertensive emergency)

marker_tokens: Plasma Renin (Direct) - used for secondary hypertension workup

fields.Definition: Persistently elevated blood pressure, which can be primary (essential) or secondary to an identifiable cause such as a renin-related hormonal disorder. Note: blood pressure itself is a vital-sign measurement, not a lab test - the only NG lab marker currently sitting under the 'Hypertension' profile is Plasma Renin, which is specifically used to investigate secondary causes, not to screen for hypertension itself.
fields.Common Symptoms: Usually asymptomatic ("silent"); severe cases: headache, vision changes, chest pain
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Plasma Renin (Direct) - used for secondary hypertension workup, not primary screening
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Repeated BP readings meeting hypertension thresholds; Plasma Renin plus Aldosterone to investigate suspected secondary causes
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Elevated Plasma Renin pattern suggesting a renin-mediated (renovascular) cause in a patient with confirmed hypertension
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly/emergency if very high BP with symptoms (hypertensive emergency)
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic; well managed with lifestyle and medication in most cases
fields.Possible Complications: Stroke, heart attack, kidney disease, heart failure if uncontrolled
fields.External Risk Factors: High sodium diet, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, high alcohol intake, smoking, stress
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Strong family history component
fields.Other Important Factors: Age-related risk increase; pregnancy-related hypertension (preeclampsia) is a distinct condition
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Primary vs. secondary hypertension causes (renal artery stenosis, hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Sodium reduction, weight management, exercise, alcohol moderation
fields.Recommended Next Step: Primary care management; nephrology/endocrinology referral if secondary cause suspected

fields.Definition: A primary cancer of the liver, most often arising in patients with chronic liver disease (cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B/C).
fields.Common Symptoms: Weight loss, abdominal pain/swelling, jaundice, often asymptomatic in early stages
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Elevated AFP correlated with liver imaging (ultrasound/CT/MRI) showing a mass; biopsy in equivocal cases
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Rising or markedly elevated AFP in a patient with chronic liver disease or a liver mass on imaging
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly on new liver mass or rapidly rising AFP

fields.Possible Complications: Liver failure, metastasis if diagnosed late
fields.External Risk Factors: Chronic Hepatitis B/C, alcohol-related cirrhosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of liver disease in the context of hereditary hemochromatosis or hepatitis
fields.Other Important Factors: Regular AFP + ultrasound surveillance recommended for known cirrhosis patients
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Benign liver lesions, metastatic cancer to the liver, germ cell tumors (also raise AFP)
