urgency.escalation: emergency if severe/rapid-onset with confusion or seizures
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe/rapid-onset with confusion or seizures

fields.Definition: A serum sodium level outside the normal range, reflecting an imbalance between body water and sodium rather than a disease in itself; low sodium (hyponatremia) is far more common than high sodium (hypernatremia).
fields.Common Symptoms: Often none if mild; nausea, headache, confusion, muscle cramps, lethargy; severe cases can cause seizures or altered consciousness
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Serum osmolality, urine sodium/osmolality, volume status assessment to determine underlying cause
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Sodium persistently outside 136-145 mmol/L, especially with associated symptoms or rapid change
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe/rapid-onset with confusion or seizures
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Usually reversible once the underlying cause (fluid loss, overhydration, medication, hormonal) is identified and corrected
fields.Possible Complications: Cerebral edema, osmotic demyelination if corrected too quickly, seizures, falls in the elderly
fields.External Risk Factors: Diuretic use, excessive water intake, heat exposure/dehydration, certain medications (SSRIs, some anticonvulsants)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not typically hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in elderly patients and those on diuretics; correction rate matters clinically (rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia is dangerous)
fields.Differential Diagnoses: SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, heart/liver/kidney failure with fluid overload, diabetes insipidus
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoid excessive fluid intake without electrolyte replacement during prolonged exertion; review diuretic dosing periodically
fields.Recommended Next Step: Physician review of medications and fluid status; nephrology/endocrinology referral if recurrent or severe
fields.Source / Reference: General nephrology/electrolyte references (e.g. Adrogue-Madias framework for sodium disorders); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe (very high or very low) or ECG changes present
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe (very high or very low) or ECG changes present

fields.Definition: A serum potassium level outside the normal range; both high and low potassium can directly affect heart rhythm and muscle function, making this one of the more clinically urgent electrolyte findings.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often silent until levels are markedly abnormal; muscle weakness, cramps, palpitations, fatigue; severe cases can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Repeat serum potassium (to rule out lab artifact/hemolysis), ECG, renal function tests, review of medications
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Potassium significantly outside the reference range, particularly with ECG changes or use of potassium-affecting medications (ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe (very high or very low) or ECG changes present
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reversible once the cause is corrected; recurrence is common if the underlying driver (kidney disease, medications) persists
fields.Possible Complications: Cardiac arrhythmia, cardiac arrest in severe cases, muscle paralysis (severe hypokalemia)
fields.External Risk Factors: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, laxative or diuretic misuse, poor dietary intake, excessive supplementation
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare inherited periodic paralysis syndromes
fields.Other Important Factors: Kidney function strongly influences potassium handling; more concerning in patients with pre-existing heart disease
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Renal failure/acute kidney injury, adrenal disorders (Addison’s, hyperaldosteronism), medication effect, metabolic acidosis/alkalosis shifting potassium
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Routine monitoring for patients on relevant medications; dietary review if levels borderline
fields.Recommended Next Step: Prompt physician review, ECG if markedly abnormal; nephrology referral if recurrent
fields.Source / Reference: General nephrology/cardiology references on potassium disorders; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion)

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe/rapid-onset hyponatremia with confusion or seizures
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe/rapid-onset hyponatremia with confusion or seizures

fields.Disease/Medical Condition: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion)
fields.Definition: A condition where the body releases too much antidiuretic hormone, causing the kidneys to retain excess water and dilute blood sodium, typically presenting as hyponatremia with concentrated urine.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often the symptoms of hyponatremia itself - nausea, headache, confusion, lethargy; may be asymptomatic if mild and chronic
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Serum and urine osmolality, urine sodium, exclusion of adrenal/thyroid/renal causes, assessment for underlying trigger (lung/CNS disease, medications, cancer)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine (high urine osmolality) despite normal volume status
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe/rapid-onset hyponatremia with confusion or seizures
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Depends on the underlying cause; often reversible if the trigger (medication, infection, tumor) is identified and addressed
fields.Possible Complications: Severe hyponatremia, seizures, complications from correcting sodium too quickly
fields.External Risk Factors: Certain medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, some chemotherapy), lung infections, CNS disorders
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not typically hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Can be paraneoplastic (associated with lung cancer); more common in elderly patients on multiple medications
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Other causes of hyponatremia (adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, heart/liver/kidney failure, diuretic use)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No specific primary prevention; review of contributing medications when recurrent
fields.Recommended Next Step: Endocrinology or internal medicine referral to identify and treat the underlying cause
fields.Source / Reference: Standard endocrinology references on ADH/water balance disorders; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, respiratory compromise)
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, respiratory compromise)

fields.Definition: A disturbance in the body’s normal acid-base balance, reflected indirectly through electrolyte patterns (e.g. anion gap) rather than a disease in itself.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue, rapid/deep breathing (acidosis), confusion, muscle twitching or cramps; can be asymptomatic if mild
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Sodium, Potassium, Chloride (used to estimate anion gap)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Arterial or venous blood gas, serum bicarbonate, anion gap calculation, lactate
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Electrolyte pattern suggesting a wide anion gap or clinical context (vomiting, diarrhea, kidney disease, uncontrolled diabetes) consistent with acid-base disturbance
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; emergency if severe (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, respiratory compromise)
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Reversible with treatment of the underlying cause; severity depends entirely on that cause
fields.Possible Complications: Cardiac arrhythmia, organ dysfunction if severe and untreated
fields.External Risk Factors: Prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, uncontrolled diabetes, kidney disease, certain medications/toxins
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare inherited renal tubular acidosis syndromes
fields.Other Important Factors: Almost always secondary to another condition rather than a standalone diagnosis
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Diabetic ketoacidosis, renal tubular acidosis, kidney failure, severe diarrhea/vomiting, toxin ingestion, respiratory disorders (for alkalosis)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Manage underlying conditions (diabetes, kidney disease); avoid unmonitored use of antacids/diuretics
fields.Recommended Next Step: Physician evaluation with blood gas testing to identify the underlying driver
fields.Source / Reference: Standard acid-base physiology references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: urgent if severe flare, significant bleeding, or bowel obstruction signs
urgency.raw: Needs specialist management; urgent if severe flare, significant bleeding, or bowel obstruction signs

fields.Definition: A group of chronic conditions causing ongoing inflammation of the digestive tract - Crohn's disease can affect any part from mouth to anus, while ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum.
fields.Common Symptoms: Chronic or recurrent diarrhea (often with blood/mucus in UC), abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, fever during flares
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Stool analysis (occult blood), CBC, inflammatory markers
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Colonoscopy with biopsy, fecal calprotectin, imaging (MR/CT enterography for Crohn's)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Persistent diarrhea (over several weeks) with blood/mucus, unexplained weight loss, abnormal stool findings with systemic symptoms
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management; urgent if severe flare, significant bleeding, or bowel obstruction signs
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, relapsing-remitting; not curable but usually manageable with long-term treatment and monitoring
fields.Possible Complications: Strictures/bowel obstruction, fistulas (Crohn's), toxic megacolon (UC), increased colorectal cancer risk with long-standing disease, nutritional deficiencies
fields.External Risk Factors: Smoking (worsens Crohn's, may protect against UC), diet, prior GI infections
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Meaningful familial clustering; multiple genetic risk loci identified
fields.Other Important Factors: Often begins in adolescence or young adulthood; extra-intestinal manifestations (joints, skin, eyes) are common
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Irritable bowel syndrome, infectious colitis, intestinal parasitic infection, celiac disease, colorectal cancer
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No proven primary prevention; smoking cessation relevant for Crohn's; dietary management during flares
fields.Recommended Next Step: Gastroenterologist referral for colonoscopy and long-term management
fields.Source / Reference: Standard gastroenterology references (ACG/ECCO-aligned IBD guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.raw: Routine - manage symptoms

fields.Definition: A common functional gut disorder causing recurrent abdominal pain linked to changes in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both), without structural or inflammatory disease on testing.
fields.Common Symptoms: Abdominal pain/cramping relieved by defecation, bloating, altered bowel habits (diarrhea and/or constipation), mucus in stool
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Stool analysis (to exclude blood, infection, inflammation)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Primarily a diagnosis of exclusion (Rome criteria); stool tests, celiac screening, and colonoscopy used to rule out other causes
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Chronic pattern fits symptom-based criteria AND stool/blood tests show no red-flag findings (blood, marked inflammation, weight loss)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - manage symptoms
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic but not progressive or life-threatening; often fluctuates with stress, diet, and lifestyle
fields.Possible Complications: Reduced quality of life; no structural bowel damage
fields.External Risk Factors: Stress, certain foods (FODMAPs), prior GI infection (post-infectious IBS)
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Modest familial tendency
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in women; symptoms overlap significantly with other GI conditions, so red-flag features must be excluded first
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, intestinal parasitic infection, lactose/other food intolerance
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Dietary modification (e.g. low-FODMAP trial), stress management, regular physical activity
fields.Recommended Next Step: Primary care evaluation to exclude red-flag causes; gastroenterology referral if atypical or refractory
fields.Source / Reference: Standard gastroenterology references (Rome IV functional GI disorder criteria); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.raw: Routine - treat promptly

fields.Definition: Infection of the intestinal tract by parasitic worms (e.g. roundworm, hookworm) or protozoa (e.g. Giardia, Entamoeba), usually acquired through contaminated food, water, or soil.
fields.Common Symptoms: Diarrhea (sometimes with blood/mucus in amoebic infection), abdominal pain/cramping, bloating, fatigue, weight loss; can be asymptomatic
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Stool ova and parasite examination (often multiple samples), stool antigen tests, occasionally serology
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Ova, cysts, or parasites identified on stool microscopy, especially with compatible symptoms or exposure history
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - treat promptly
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Usually resolves fully with appropriate antiparasitic treatment
fields.Possible Complications: Chronic malabsorption and nutritional deficiency if untreated; invasive amoebiasis (liver abscess) in some infections
fields.External Risk Factors: Contaminated food/water, poor sanitation, travel to endemic areas, poor hand hygiene
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in areas with limited access to clean water and sanitation; children at higher risk in endemic settings
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Bacterial gastroenteritis, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, malabsorption syndrome
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Safe drinking water, food hygiene, handwashing, proper sanitation
fields.Recommended Next Step: Antiparasitic treatment as directed by a physician; repeat stool testing to confirm clearance if symptomatic
fields.Source / Reference: Standard infectious disease/parasitology references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: urgent if severe weight loss or signs of dehydration
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; urgent if severe weight loss or signs of dehydration

fields.Definition: A condition where the intestine fails to properly absorb nutrients, fats, vitamins, or minerals from food, leading to deficiencies and gastrointestinal symptoms; a shared endpoint of several underlying diseases rather than a single disease itself.
fields.Common Symptoms: Chronic diarrhea, bloating, greasy/foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea), weight loss, fatigue, signs of vitamin/mineral deficiency
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Stool analysis (fecal fat), Vitamin D/B12/Folate, Iron studies, Total Protein
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Fecal fat quantification, celiac serology, pancreatic function testing, small bowel imaging/endoscopy with biopsy depending on suspected cause
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea plus multiple vitamin/mineral deficiencies or unexplained weight loss
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; urgent if severe weight loss or signs of dehydration
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Depends entirely on the underlying cause (celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, IBD, prior bowel surgery); often improves once that cause is treated
fields.Possible Complications: Malnutrition, anemia, bone disease (from fat-soluble vitamin deficiency), growth failure in children
fields.External Risk Factors: Prior GI surgery, chronic pancreatitis, prolonged untreated celiac disease
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Depends on underlying cause (e.g. celiac disease has genetic links)
fields.Other Important Factors: Can present subtly in early stages; often identified through deficiency workup rather than GI symptoms alone
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Celiac disease, chronic pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal parasitic infection, short bowel syndrome
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Manage underlying causes promptly; nutritional support/supplementation as directed
fields.Recommended Next Step: Gastroenterology referral to identify the underlying cause
fields.Source / Reference: Standard gastroenterology/nutrition references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly if high fever, bloody stool, or signs of dehydration
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if high fever, bloody stool, or signs of dehydration

fields.Definition: Acute intestinal infection caused by bacteria such as Salmonella or Shigella, typically acquired from contaminated food or water, causing inflammation of the gut lining.
fields.Common Symptoms: Diarrhea (may be bloody with Shigella), abdominal cramps, fever, nausea/vomiting; usually acute onset
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Stool analysis (microscopy for white/red blood cells)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Stool culture, stool PCR panel where available
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Acute bloody or high-volume diarrhea with fever, especially after a known exposure (contaminated food/water, travel, sick contacts)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if high fever, bloody stool, or signs of dehydration
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Usually self-limited over days to about a week; can be more severe in young children, elderly, or immunocompromised patients
fields.Possible Complications: Dehydration, and rarely bacteremia, reactive arthritis, or hemolytic uremic syndrome (certain strains)
fields.External Risk Factors: Contaminated food/water, poor sanitation, travel to endemic areas
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Highly contagious in close-contact settings; antibiotic use is selective and depends on severity/organism
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Viral gastroenteritis, intestinal parasitic infection, inflammatory bowel disease flare
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Safe food/water practices, handwashing, prompt isolation of infected individuals in shared settings
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hydration and physician evaluation; stool culture if symptoms are severe or persistent
fields.Source / Reference: Standard infectious disease references (CDC/WHO-aligned enteric infection guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: Thalassemia (Trait/Major)
synonyms: Thalassemia trait; Thalassemia major; Cooley's anemia (beta-thalassemia major)

urgency.escalation: Routine - identify underlying cause (trait, usually asymptomatic)
urgency.raw: Needs specialist management (major form); Routine - identify underlying cause (trait, usually asymptomatic)

fields.Related Profile(s): Blood Disorder, Hemoglobin Electrophoresis, Anemia Studies
fields.Synonyms / AKA: Thalassemia trait; Thalassemia major; Cooley's anemia (beta-thalassemia major)
fields.Definition: An inherited blood disorder causing reduced or abnormal production of hemoglobin chains, ranging from a mild, often symptomless "trait" to a severe, transfusion-dependent "major" form.
fields.Common Symptoms: Trait: often none, mild fatigue. Major: severe fatigue, pallor, poor growth in children, bone deformities, enlarged spleen
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Hemoglobin, RBC indices (low MCV out of proportion to hemoglobin is a classic clue), Hemoglobin electrophoresis
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC showing abnormal hemoglobin fractions, genetic testing for globin gene mutations
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Microcytic anemia (low MCV) that doesn't fully correct with iron, especially with a relevant family/ethnic background
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management (major form); Routine - identify underlying cause (trait, usually asymptomatic)
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Trait is typically lifelong but benign; major form is chronic and requires ongoing transfusion/chelation management
fields.Possible Complications: Iron overload (especially with repeated transfusions), growth delay, bone deformities, heart/liver damage from iron overload in major form
fields.External Risk Factors: Not lifestyle-related; inherited condition
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Autosomal recessive inheritance; strongly associated with Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Southeast Asian ancestry
fields.Other Important Factors: Important to distinguish from iron deficiency anemia, since iron supplementation is not appropriate (and can be harmful) in thalassemia
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Iron deficiency anemia, sickle cell disease, other hemoglobinopathies
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Genetic counseling for carriers, especially before family planning
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hematology referral for confirmation and, for major form, ongoing specialist management
fields.Source / Reference: Standard hematology references (WHO/Thalassemia International Federation-aligned guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: Hemophilia (A/B)
synonyms: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency); Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe active bleeding, especially into a joint, muscle, or head
urgency.raw: Needs specialist management; emergency if severe active bleeding, especially into a joint, muscle, or head

fields.Synonyms / AKA: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency); Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease)
fields.Definition: An inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of a specific blood clotting factor (Factor VIII in Hemophilia A, Factor IX in Hemophilia B), leading to prolonged or spontaneous bleeding.
fields.Common Symptoms: Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after injury/surgery, spontaneous joint or muscle bleeding, in severe cases bleeding with minimal or no trauma
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Prothrombin Time/APTT (typically prolonged APTT with normal PT)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Specific clotting factor assays (Factor VIII/IX levels), genetic testing
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Prolonged APTT with normal PT, especially with a personal/family history of unusual bleeding or joint bleeds
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management; emergency if severe active bleeding, especially into a joint, muscle, or head
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic, lifelong condition; severity (mild/moderate/severe) is fairly stable within a family and determines bleeding frequency
fields.Possible Complications: Joint damage from recurrent bleeds (hemophilic arthropathy), life-threatening bleeding (intracranial, internal)
fields.External Risk Factors: Not lifestyle-related; contact sports/trauma increase bleeding risk
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: X-linked recessive inheritance; predominantly affects males, with female carriers
fields.Other Important Factors: Severity is classified by residual factor activity level; management typically involves factor replacement therapy
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Von Willebrand disease, other clotting factor deficiencies, acquired coagulopathy (e.g. liver disease)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoid contact sports/high trauma-risk activities in known cases; genetic counseling for carriers
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hematology referral for factor level testing and specialist management
fields.Source / Reference: Standard hematology references (World Federation of Hemophilia-aligned guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly if active/heavy bleeding
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if active/heavy bleeding

fields.Definition: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor, a protein needed for normal platelet function and clotting.
fields.Common Symptoms: Easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, heavy menstrual bleeding, prolonged bleeding after cuts, dental work, or surgery
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Prothrombin Time/APTT (often normal or mildly prolonged APTT)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity assays, Factor VIII level
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Recurrent mucocutaneous bleeding (nosebleeds, heavy periods, easy bruising) with a family history of similar symptoms
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if active/heavy bleeding
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic but usually mild to moderate; many people manage well with awareness and treatment around procedures
fields.Possible Complications: Significant bleeding with surgery, dental procedures, or childbirth if unrecognized
fields.External Risk Factors: Not lifestyle-related
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Usually autosomal dominant inheritance; strong family history is typical
fields.Other Important Factors: Frequently underdiagnosed, especially in women with heavy menstrual bleeding attributed to other causes
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Hemophilia, platelet function disorders, other causes of heavy menstrual bleeding
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Inform care providers before surgery/dental work; avoid unnecessary NSAIDs/blood thinners
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hematology referral for specific factor testing
fields.Source / Reference: Standard hematology references (ISTH-aligned VWD guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: emergency if severe infection or bleeding
urgency.raw: Needs specialist management; emergency if severe infection or bleeding

fields.Related Profile(s): Blood Disorder, Anemia Studies, Blood Counts
fields.Definition: A rare but serious condition where the bone marrow fails to produce enough new blood cells of all types (red cells, white cells, and platelets), leading to pancytopenia.
fields.Common Symptoms: Fatigue and pallor (from anemia), frequent infections (from low white cells), easy bruising/bleeding (from low platelets)
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Hemoglobin, WBC count, Platelet Count (a low count across all three lines is the key pattern)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellular marrow, exclusion of other causes of pancytopenia
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Simultaneous low hemoglobin, low white cell count, and low platelet count (pancytopenia) without an obvious alternate cause
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs specialist management; emergency if severe infection or bleeding
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Can range from mild to severe/life-threatening; treatable with immunosuppressive therapy or bone marrow transplant depending on severity
fields.Possible Complications: Life-threatening infection, severe bleeding, dependence on transfusions
fields.External Risk Factors: Certain medications, toxins (e.g. benzene), viral infections, autoimmune conditions
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare inherited forms exist (e.g. Fanconi anemia), though most cases are acquired
fields.Other Important Factors: Can occur at any age; often idiopathic (no identifiable cause found)
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Myelodysplastic syndrome, leukemia, other causes of pancytopenia (severe B12/folate deficiency, hypersplenism)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoid known marrow-toxic exposures where possible; no proven primary prevention for idiopathic cases
fields.Recommended Next Step: Urgent hematology referral for bone marrow evaluation
fields.Source / Reference: Standard hematology references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: Hemoglobin C/E Disease (HbC/HbE)
synonyms: HbC disease; HbE disease; Hemoglobin C/E trait

urgency.raw: Routine - identify underlying cause

fields.Synonyms / AKA: HbC disease; HbE disease; Hemoglobin C/E trait
fields.Definition: Inherited hemoglobin variants (HbC and HbE) that can cause mild to moderate anemia; trait forms are typically mild and often found incidentally, while combined forms with other hemoglobin variants can be more significant.
fields.Common Symptoms: Trait forms are often asymptomatic; combined/homozygous forms may cause mild fatigue and pallor
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC identifying the specific variant, genetic testing if needed
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Mild microcytic anemia with an abnormal hemoglobin fraction on electrophoresis not explained by iron deficiency or thalassemia alone
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - identify underlying cause
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Usually mild and compatible with a normal lifespan; more significant when combined with other hemoglobin disorders
fields.Possible Complications: Mild hemolysis and gallstones in some homozygous cases; generally good prognosis otherwise
fields.External Risk Factors: Not lifestyle-related
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Autosomal recessive inheritance; HbE particularly common in Southeast Asian populations, HbC in West African populations
fields.Other Important Factors: Important to distinguish from thalassemia and iron deficiency, which can look similar on basic blood counts
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Thalassemia trait, iron deficiency anemia, sickle cell trait
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Genetic counseling for carriers considering family planning, especially if a partner also carries a hemoglobin variant
fields.Recommended Next Step: Hematology referral for confirmation if found incidentally
fields.Source / Reference: Standard hematology references on hemoglobinopathies; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: urgent if new fracture occurs
urgency.raw: Routine - manage long-term; urgent if new fracture occurs

fields.Definition: A condition where bones become weak and porous due to loss of bone density and quality, significantly increasing the risk of fractures, often with no symptoms until a fracture occurs.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often none until a fracture occurs; loss of height, stooped posture, or back pain from vertebral compression fractures over time
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Calcium, Vitamin D, Phosphorus (used to assess bone-relevant metabolic status)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: DEXA bone density scan (the actual diagnostic test), assessment of fracture risk (e.g. FRAX score)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low bone-relevant markers (e.g. Vitamin D) in an at-risk individual (postmenopausal woman, older adult, prior fragility fracture)
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - manage long-term; urgent if new fracture occurs
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic and progressive if untreated, but fracture risk can be substantially reduced with treatment and lifestyle measures
fields.Possible Complications: Fragility fractures (hip, spine, wrist), chronic pain, loss of mobility/independence, especially after hip fracture
fields.External Risk Factors: Low calcium/vitamin D intake, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, excess alcohol, prolonged corticosteroid use
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Family history of osteoporosis or fragility fracture increases risk
fields.Other Important Factors: Much more common in postmenopausal women due to estrogen decline; also occurs in men and secondary to other conditions
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Osteomalacia, multiple myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, metastatic bone disease
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate calcium/vitamin D intake, weight-bearing exercise, smoking cessation, fall-prevention measures
fields.Recommended Next Step: DEXA scan and physician review, especially for postmenopausal women or those with a fragility fracture
fields.Source / Reference: Standard endocrinology/bone health references (Endocrine Society-aligned osteoporosis guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.raw: Routine - treat and monitor

fields.Definition: A condition where bones become soft and weak due to defective bone mineralization, most commonly from vitamin D deficiency - called rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
fields.Common Symptoms: Bone pain and tenderness, muscle weakness, in children: bowed legs, delayed growth, and skeletal deformities
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Vitamin D level plus X-ray findings (e.g. Looser's zones in osteomalacia, growth plate changes in rickets); occasionally bone biopsy
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Low Vitamin D with low or low-normal Calcium/Phosphorus, especially with bone pain or, in children, growth/skeletal changes
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - treat and monitor
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Generally reversible with vitamin D and calcium repletion, especially if caught before permanent skeletal deformity develops
fields.Possible Complications: Permanent bone deformity (especially in children if untreated), fractures, growth impairment
fields.External Risk Factors: Limited sun exposure, poor dietary vitamin D/calcium intake, malabsorption conditions
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare inherited forms (e.g. vitamin D-resistant rickets) exist
fields.Other Important Factors: More common in regions with limited sunlight, darker skin (reduced vitamin D synthesis), and exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Osteoporosis, malabsorption syndrome, chronic kidney disease-related bone disease, hyperparathyroidism
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Adequate sun exposure and dietary vitamin D/calcium, supplementation where indicated (especially infants and at-risk groups)
fields.Recommended Next Step: Vitamin D/calcium repletion under physician guidance; pediatric referral for suspected rickets
fields.Source / Reference: Standard endocrinology references (Endocrine Society-aligned vitamin D guidance); AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: Paget's Disease of Bone

urgency.raw: Routine - manage long-term

marker_tokens: included here as part of the same bone-metabolism marker set)

fields.Definition: A chronic condition in which bone remodeling becomes disorganized, leading to bone that is enlarged, misshapen, and structurally weaker than normal, usually affecting one or a few bones rather than the whole skeleton.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; bone pain, deformity, or joint pain when a weight-bearing bone is affected
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Calcium, Phosphorus (usually normal; included here as part of the same bone-metabolism marker set)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Elevated alkaline phosphatase, characteristic X-ray findings, bone scan
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Normal calcium/phosphorus but clinical suspicion (bone pain/deformity) in an older adult, particularly with an elevated alkaline phosphatase on other testing
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Routine - manage long-term
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Chronic and slowly progressive; often manageable with treatment that reduces bone turnover
fields.Possible Complications: Bone deformity, fractures, osteoarthritis in nearby joints, rarely hearing loss (skull involvement) or, very rarely, bone cancer
fields.External Risk Factors: Not strongly linked to lifestyle factors
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Meaningful genetic component; more common with a family history
fields.Other Important Factors: More common with increasing age and in certain populations (e.g. more common in people of British/European descent)
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Osteoporosis, metastatic bone disease, hyperparathyroidism
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No proven primary prevention; adequate calcium/vitamin D generally advised
fields.Recommended Next Step: Physician review; endocrinology or orthopedic referral if symptomatic
fields.Source / Reference: Standard bone metabolism references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

diseases.name: Male Infertility (Oligospermia/Azoospermia)
synonyms: Oligospermia (low sperm count); Azoospermia (no sperm present); Male factor infertility

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing

fields.Synonyms / AKA: Oligospermia (low sperm count); Azoospermia (no sperm present); Male factor infertility
fields.Definition: A reduced or absent sperm count that impairs a couple's ability to conceive, ranging from mildly low counts (oligospermia) to a complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate (azoospermia).
fields.Common Symptoms: Usually no physical symptoms; identified through difficulty conceiving or a semen analysis performed for that reason
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Repeat semen analysis (results vary day to day), hormone panel (testosterone, FSH, LH), scrotal ultrasound, genetic testing in select cases
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Sperm concentration below the reference range on semen analysis, especially on repeat testing
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Highly variable - some causes are reversible (e.g. hormonal, varicocele-related) while others require assisted reproduction
fields.Possible Complications: Difficulty or inability to conceive naturally; psychological/relationship impact
fields.External Risk Factors: Smoking, heavy alcohol use, heat exposure (e.g. frequent hot tub use), certain medications, obesity
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Some genetic causes (e.g. Y-chromosome microdeletions, Klinefelter syndrome) especially in azoospermia
fields.Other Important Factors: Male factor contributes to roughly half of couples' infertility cases; often coexists with a female-factor cause
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Varicocele-related infertility, hormonal causes (Male Hypogonadism), obstructive causes, prior infection (e.g. mumps orchitis)
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoid smoking/excess alcohol/heat exposure to the scrotum, maintain healthy weight
fields.Recommended Next Step: Urology or fertility specialist referral for further evaluation
fields.Source / Reference: Standard urology/reproductive medicine references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing

fields.Definition: A condition where the proportion of actively motile sperm in the semen is below normal, reducing the likelihood of sperm reaching and fertilizing an egg.
fields.Common Symptoms: No physical symptoms; identified through semen analysis performed for fertility evaluation
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Repeat semen analysis, assessment for infection or antisperm antibodies, evaluation of lifestyle/exposure factors
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Motile sperm percentage below the reference range on semen analysis, especially on repeat testing
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly if trying to conceive and abnormal on repeat testing
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Variable; can improve with treatment of an underlying cause (infection, lifestyle factors) or may require assisted reproductive techniques
fields.Possible Complications: Reduced natural fertility
fields.External Risk Factors: Smoking, heavy alcohol use, heat exposure, genital infection, prolonged abstinence before testing
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Rare structural sperm defects can be hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: Often coexists with other semen abnormalities (low count, abnormal morphology)
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Male infertility (oligospermia/azoospermia), genital tract infection (e.g. prostatitis/epididymitis), varicocele
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: Avoid smoking/excess alcohol/heat exposure; treat any underlying genital infection
fields.Recommended Next Step: Urology or fertility specialist referral
fields.Source / Reference: Standard urology/reproductive medicine references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.

urgency.escalation: seek care promptly for new/painful scrotal swelling
urgency.raw: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly for new/painful scrotal swelling

fields.Definition: An enlargement of the veins within the scrotum (similar to varicose veins), which can raise scrotal temperature and impair sperm production, making it one of the more common correctable causes of male infertility.
fields.Common Symptoms: Often none; occasionally a dull scrotal ache or a visible/palpable "bag of worms" swelling above the testicle, typically on the left side
fields.Related Markers/Tests: Semen analysis (may show reduced count and/or motility)
fields.Confirmatory/Diagnostic Tests: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler (confirms and grades the varicocele)
fields.High-Risk Indicators: Abnormal semen analysis with a palpable scrotal varicocele on examination
fields.Severity/Urgency Level: Needs monitoring; seek care promptly for new/painful scrotal swelling
fields.Prognosis / Typical Course: Often improves with surgical correction (varicocelectomy) in men with associated infertility, though not all men with a varicocele have fertility issues
fields.Possible Complications: Reduced fertility, testicular atrophy in some cases
fields.External Risk Factors: Not strongly linked to lifestyle factors
fields.Genetic/Family History Factors: Not typically hereditary
fields.Other Important Factors: One of the most common identifiable and treatable causes of male infertility
fields.Differential Diagnoses: Male infertility from other causes, epididymitis, inguinal hernia
fields.Prevention/Lifestyle Guidance: No proven primary prevention
fields.Recommended Next Step: Urology referral for evaluation and discussion of treatment options
fields.Source / Reference: Standard urology references; AI-drafted, not individually verified.
